newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy prepares troops to help fight Naples mob.
newsitem.headline: Italy prepares troops to help fight Naples mob.

text.p: The Italian government on Friday approved the deployment of 500 troops to Naples to help police crack down on gangsters who are plaguing the southern port city with turf wars.

The soldiers will take over guard duties around Naples so police officers can focus on halting a wave of mob violence that has swept the city, Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano said after a cabinet meeting approved the plan.
Napolitano told reporters the deployment would cost seven billion lire ($4.1 million) and last until year-end.
Italian media said the army might arrive as early as Sunday, with most residents in the area ready to welcome them.

"I hope this will be able to exorcise the senseless cruelty that disturbs the lives of innocent and defenceless people in our cities," said Antonio Napoletano, the Bishop of Sessa Aurunca, a small village near Naples.

Local authorities were also pleased, saying the deployment would show Italy was serious about fighting the Naples Mafia, known as the Camorra, which has often received less public attention than more famous mob gangs on the neighbouring island of Sicily.
"This is an important signal because it means the serious problem of the Camorra is being made a national commitment," Italy's top anti-mob prosecutor Pier Luigi Vigna told the daily La Repubblica.

General Nicola Vozza, commander of the military's southern forces, said in a radio interview that the troops will use armoured transport "similar to that which police use when guarding streets or stadiums in sensitive situations."
Some 86 people have been killed and dozens injured since the start of the year as rival Camorra clans have been waging wars to expand their territorial control.

The battle has increasingly spilled onto the streets of Naples and there was public outrage last month after a young woman was killed by a stray bullet as she walked home with her six-year-old son in an affluent neighbourhood.

The decision to send troops was announced on Monday after a weekend of terror in which two suspected mobsters were mowed down in broad daylight and a number of innocent bystanders, including an eight-year-old girl, were hurt in shootouts.
Later on Friday, police arrested a suspected Camorra boss who operated in the area where the girl had been wounded.
Local merchants feared the presence of troops in Naples' historic centre would hurt a tourism boom the city has nurtured over the last four years.
"I hope we don't go back to the times of (Fascist dictator Benito) Mussolini, and that tourists will visit anyway," Edoardo di Giorgio, owner of a Naples cafe, told Reuters.
But Naples Mayor Antonio Bassolino said the operation would be similar to the one that quietly guarded a Group of Seven summit meeting held in the city in 1994.
"No one noticed the troops then," Bassolino told Reuters. "We will continue strolling through the streets of a city in which people live more in the open air than any other in Italy."

Italy has used troops before in various parts of the country to quell crime waves. Troops are still stationed in Sicily five years after being called in following the mafia assassination of two leading magistrates.
